translations.work.assembler.tagline.text: A desktop CPU simulator that assembles a 47-instruction set and executes it one microcode step at a time, with the datapath drawn and lit as it goes.
translations.work.assembler.summary.text: A .NET MAUI app whose simulator core knows nothing about the screen. It reports what each microcode step touched, and the schematic decides how to light it.
translations.work.assembler.note.text: Only the presenter may talk to more than one pane. That is what lets me test the state machine with no UI running.
translations.work.assembler.fact.1.label: Role
translations.work.assembler.fact.1.value: Sole author, layered port of an educational simulator
translations.work.assembler.fact.2.label: Shape
translations.work.assembler.fact.2.value: Four projects, dependency arrow one way, domain depends on nothing
translations.work.assembler.fact.3.label: Instruction set
translations.work.assembler.fact.3.value: 47 mnemonics in four encoding classes, four addressing modes
translations.work.assembler.fact.4.label: Targets
translations.work.assembler.fact.4.value: Windows and Mac Catalyst, English and Romanian
translations.work.assembler.fact.5.label: Tests
translations.work.assembler.fact.5.value: 83 test methods over 80 data rows, in three test projects
translations.work.assembler.fact.6.label: Gate
translations.work.assembler.fact.6.value: StyleCop and .NET analyzers, warnings as errors
translations.work.assembler.fact.7.label: Source
translations.work.assembler.media.label: assembler · desktop simulator
translations.work.assembler.media.alt: The Assembler desktop app: source editor, processor schematic with buses and registers, and stacked memory, machine code and microcode panes.
translations.work.assembler.page.text: Assembler in detail: four layers with the dependency arrow pointing one way, a pure simulator core publishing events over a channel, and a hand-drawn datapath that lights up as the microcode advances.
translations.work.assembler.overview.title: Overview
translations.work.assembler.overview.usecase.text: A student writes ten lines of assembly, presses Step, and watches a value travel along the bus into a register.
translations.work.assembler.overview.item.1: Write or open assembly source in the editor
translations.work.assembler.overview.item.3: Run, pause, step or reset, at a speed you choose
translations.work.assembler.overview.item.4: See the active buses and registers light up on the processor schematic
translations.work.assembler.overview.callout.label: Engineering note
translations.work.assembler.architecture.title: Architecture
translations.work.assembler.architecture.text.1: Four layers, and a domain that could run from a console tomorrow.
translations.work.assembler.architecture.caption.1: Dependency direction: Maui to Presentation to UseCases to Domain
translations.work.assembler.architecture.item.1: The domain uses no UI framework and starts no timers. Delay comes from an injected clock.
translations.work.assembler.architecture.item.2: Every effect leaves the domain as a typed event over a channel.
translations.work.assembler.architecture.item.3: I chose MVP over plain MVVM so one presenter holds the coordination, not every pane.
translations.work.assembler.architecture.item.4: The only packages are MAUI and CommunityToolkit.Mvvm. The schematic is drawn by hand.
translations.work.assembler.domain.title: Domain design
translations.work.assembler.domain.text.1: An instruction set where the opcode is derived, not looked up.
translations.work.assembler.domain.item.1: 47 mnemonics in four encoding classes, four addressing modes, sixteen registers.
translations.work.assembler.domain.item.2: Each instruction runs as a microcode program that names the exact bus it uses.
translations.work.assembler.domain.item.3: The domain says "the S bus was activated", never "highlight this", so the drawing can change without touching the simulator.
translations.work.assembler.flow.title: Data and control flow
translations.work.assembler.flow.text.1: One press of Step, from the button to the lit bus.
translations.work.assembler.flow.item.1: The presenter fires a trigger at the state machine. A rejected transition does nothing.
translations.work.assembler.flow.item.2: The simulator fetches, decodes and runs one instruction's microcode.
translations.work.assembler.flow.item.3: Each step publishes what it touched: bus, registers, flags.
translations.work.assembler.flow.item.4: The presenter routes each event to the open panes, and the schematic redraws.
translations.work.assembler.flow.callout.label: Why a state machine drives it
translations.work.assembler.flow.callout.text: A few booleans like isRunning and isPaused work until two of them are true at once. Named states make the impossible combinations impossible.
translations.work.assembler.testing.title: Testing strategy
translations.work.assembler.testing.text.1: Three test projects below the UI, and none above the presenter.
translations.work.assembler.testing.item.1: A golden-encoding suite pins the exact machine code each instruction assembles to.
translations.work.assembler.testing.item.2: The state machine is tested exhaustively: 42 rows, every accepted and rejected transition.
translations.work.assembler.testing.item.3: The injected clock lets a twenty-second run finish in microseconds under test.
translations.work.assembler.testing.item.4: StyleCop and .NET analyzers with warnings as errors. An undocumented member fails the build.
translations.work.assembler.changes.title: What I would change
translations.work.assembler.changes.item.1: The schematic keeps its own light palette while every other pane is dark. It should read the theme.
translations.work.assembler.changes.item.3: Nothing above the presenter is tested. An automation-driven smoke test is the realistic next gate.
translations.work.assembler.changes.item.4: The state machine has no entry or exit actions: fine at nine states, not at thirty.
translations.work.assembler.changes.item.5: The microcode catalogue is built in. Loading one from a file would help students most.
translations.work.portfolio.tagline.text: The site you are reading, prerendered to static HTML in English, German and Romanian, with a first-party analytics API that hears only from readers who consent.
translations.work.portfolio.summary.text: Every address is a real file in its own language, so a crawler, a reader without scripting and a deep link all get the page itself. Angular then hydrates the markup it was sent instead of drawing it again.
translations.work.portfolio.note.text: Every layer boundary is a lint rule rather than a convention. Shared once imported a feature, and the compiler and every test stayed green.
translations.work.portfolio.fact.1.label: Role
translations.work.portfolio.fact.1.value: Sole author, design, front end, API and deployment
translations.work.portfolio.fact.2.label: Shape
translations.work.portfolio.fact.2.value: A prerendered Angular 22 site, a .NET 10 analytics API and an admin dashboard
translations.work.portfolio.fact.3.label: Languages
translations.work.portfolio.fact.3.value: English, German and Romanian, each compiled as its own build
translations.work.portfolio.fact.4.label: Pages
translations.work.portfolio.fact.4.value: 27 pages of real HTML: nine routes in three languages
translations.work.portfolio.fact.5.label: Tests
translations.work.portfolio.fact.5.value: 636 frontend specs, 572 browser tests, 193 backend test methods
translations.work.portfolio.fact.6.label: Public repository
translations.work.portfolio.fact.6.value: The complete source of the site you are reading
translations.work.portfolio.media.label: portfolio · this site
translations.work.portfolio.media.alt: The portfolio home page in dark mode: a band of technology tags, the headline, a short introduction and the buttons to the work and to more about me.
translations.work.portfolio.page.text: The portfolio site in detail: prerendered static HTML in three languages, content as typed data, layering held by lint rules, and a consent-gated analytics API on .NET 10.
translations.work.portfolio.overview.title: Overview
translations.work.portfolio.overview.usecase.text: A recruiter opens a link to the German CV on a phone with scripting blocked. The whole CV arrives in German anyway, because the address names a file that already holds it.
translations.work.portfolio.overview.item.1: Read four case studies, the CV and the legal pages in English, German or Romanian
translations.work.portfolio.overview.item.2: Download the CV as a PDF, built in the browser
translations.work.portfolio.overview.item.3: Switch between dark and light, with the choice kept for the next visit
translations.work.portfolio.figure.usecases.alt: Use case diagram: a reader browses four case studies, opens the CV and downloads it as a PDF, switches language and theme, and accepts or declines usage statistics; only with consent does the analytics API count one view a day and record interactions in batches; the owner reviews the figures and receives a morning digest.
translations.work.portfolio.figure.usecases.caption: Everything a reader does works without the API; counting starts only once they agree.
translations.work.portfolio.overview.live.label: No separate demo
translations.work.portfolio.overview.live.text: The page you are reading is the running instance, and the repository holds all of its source.
translations.work.portfolio.overview.callout.label: Engineering note
translations.work.portfolio.architecture.title: Architecture
translations.work.portfolio.architecture.text.1: A static site that stands on its own, and an API it can do without.
translations.work.portfolio.figure.architecture.alt: Architecture diagram: the browser loads prerendered pages from Azure Static Web Apps and calls the analytics API only with consent; the API passes through Analytics.Api, Analytics.Domain and Analytics.Infrastructure to Azure Table storage; a wake job triggers the morning digest, the admin dashboard reads the same table, and the shared Common packages come from a private package feed.
translations.work.portfolio.figure.architecture.capti: Left of the dashed line is everything that still works while the API sleeps.
translations.work.portfolio.architecture.item.1: Every route is prerendered at build time, so the host is a folder of files with no server of its own.
translations.work.portfolio.architecture.item.2: Each language is its own build in its own folder, /de-DE/cv for instance, because Azure Static Web Apps cannot route on a query string.
translations.work.portfolio.architecture.item.3: The Angular app is layered data, core, shared, layout and features, the arrow pointing one way, and no feature imports another.
translations.work.portfolio.architecture.item.4: The API scales to zero, and the page never waits for it: when it does not answer, the view counter is simply absent.
translations.work.portfolio.domain.title: Domain design
translations.work.portfolio.domain.text.1: The content is typed data, so a case study that breaks the shape does not compile.
translations.work.portfolio.figure.build.alt: Pipeline diagram: typed content, translations and components go into ng build, one build per language; prerendering writes 27 pages; the sitemap, the style hashes and the host configuration are generated from that output; a folder of files goes to Azure Static Web Apps.
translations.work.portfolio.figure.build.caption: Typed content in, a folder of files out. A missing translation stops the line at ng build.
translations.work.portfolio.domain.item.1: Every string a reader sees carries a stable message id, so a new extraction never orphans a translation.
translations.work.portfolio.domain.item.2: A missing translation fails the build instead of falling back to English.
translations.work.portfolio.domain.item.3: Below the features, content comes from its own file and never the barrel, or every case study would join the first download.
translations.work.portfolio.flow.title: Data and control flow
translations.work.portfolio.flow.text.1: One visit, from the address to the view counter.
translations.work.portfolio.figure.visit.alt: Sequence diagram: the browser requests /de-DE/cv and receives prerendered HTML with its CSP; Angular hydrates the markup; after the reader accepts the consent banner, the page posts one view a day, the API resolves the country from the request, buffers the count for Azure Table and answers with the totals; interactions follow as a keepalive request; if the API does not answer, an info banner appears and the page carries on.
translations.work.portfolio.figure.visit.caption: The page has everything it needs before the first request to the API is made.
translations.work.portfolio.flow.callout.label: Why the country is not a field
translations.work.portfolio.flow.callout.text: A field in the request is one the caller controls, and the country is exactly what the caller must not control.
translations.work.portfolio.testing.title: Testing strategy
translations.work.portfolio.testing.text.1: A spec beside every unit, and browser tests against the build the host will serve.
translations.work.portfolio.testing.item.1: The run fails when a component, service, directive, pipe or util has no spec beside it.
translations.work.portfolio.testing.item.2: Playwright drives the production build on a desktop and a phone, served with the host's own routes, headers and CSP.
translations.work.portfolio.testing.item.3: Every browser test fails on a console error, an uncaught exception or a request that leaves the site.
translations.work.portfolio.testing.item.4: The .NET projects build with StyleCop and warnings as errors, and the domain references no package at all, so the compiler holds its direction.
translations.work.portfolio.changes.title: What I would change
translations.work.portfolio.changes.item.1: The case studies are TypeScript, so fixing a typo in one takes a build and a deploy.
translations.work.portfolio.changes.item.2: The development server localizes one language at a time, so checking a German page needs a second command.
translations.work.portfolio.changes.item.3: The host allows one 404 page, so a small script fetches the right language in its place. A host with a 404 per folder would not need it.
translations.work.portfolio.changes.item.4: The feature boundaries in the lint config are listed by hand: a new feature means editing the config as well.
translations.work.stack86.tagline.text: A browser IDE that compiles nine languages down to 8086 assembly, then runs the result on an emulator you can single-step.
translations.work.stack86.summary.text: Compilation runs on the server, where each language is checked by its own toolchain. Execution runs in your browser, one instruction at a time, with registers, flags, stack and memory on screen.
translations.work.stack86.note.text: Seven front ends lower to the same three-address code, and C++ and TypeScript are transpiled into two of them. A new language needs a parser, not another code generator.
translations.work.stack86.fact.1.label: Role
translations.work.stack86.fact.1.value: Sole author, backend, frontend and toolchain
translations.work.stack86.fact.2.label: Shape
translations.work.stack86.fact.2.value: ASP.NET Core modular monolith plus an Angular 22 SPA
translations.work.stack86.fact.3.label: Languages in
translations.work.stack86.fact.3.value: C, C++, C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python, Rust, TypeScript
translations.work.stack86.fact.4.label: Target
translations.work.stack86.fact.4.value: 8086 assembly, executed by a browser emulator
translations.work.stack86.fact.5.label: Tests
translations.work.stack86.fact.5.value: 956 backend test methods, 864 frontend specs, 100 end to end
translations.work.stack86.fact.6.label: Public repository
translations.work.stack86.fact.6.value: A reduced variant: sign-in and persistence removed
translations.work.stack86.media.label: stack86 · compiler & emulator
translations.work.stack86.media.alt: The Stack86 IDE: C source on the left, the generated 8086 assembly on the right, and a build log reporting the pipeline.
translations.work.stack86.page.text: Stack86 in detail: nine languages lowered through seven front ends to one intermediate representation, a CQRS compilation pipeline, and an 8086 emulator that runs in the browser.
translations.work.stack86.overview.title: Overview
translations.work.stack86.overview.usecase.text: You have written a for loop ten thousand times. Stack86 shows you what the machine actually does with it.
translations.work.stack86.overview.item.1: Write in C, C++, C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python, Rust or TypeScript
translations.work.stack86.overview.item.3: Read the 8086 assembly it compiles to
translations.work.stack86.overview.item.4: Step through it and watch registers, flags, stack and memory change
translations.work.stack86.figure.usecases.alt: Use case diagram: a visitor signs up and signs in with two-factor authentication; a user writes code in one of nine languages, compiles it with a live build log and steps through the result in the emulator; the languages' own toolchains check every build.
translations.work.stack86.figure.usecases.caption: A trial licence compiles C; a full licence compiles all nine languages.
translations.work.stack86.overview.live.label: Try it
translations.work.stack86.overview.live.text: The public instance runs the full compiler. Sign-in and saving are switched off, so nothing you write is kept.
translations.work.stack86.overview.callout.label: Engineering note
translations.work.stack86.architecture.title: Architecture
translations.work.stack86.architecture.text.1: A modular monolith with one dependency direction and one deliberate process boundary.
translations.work.stack86.figure.architecture.alt: Architecture diagram: the Angular client calls Stack86.Web over HTTPS and receives the build as NDJSON; Web, Api, Logic and Data depend downward onto SQL Server, which holds identity only; Logic calls the external toolchains through Polly; the 8086 emulator runs in the browser.
translations.work.stack86.figure.architecture.caption: The dashed line is the process boundary: compile on the server, execute in the browser.
translations.work.stack86.architecture.item.1: Compilation stays on the server, where each language is checked by its own toolchain: TCC, javac, rustc, gofmt, Node, Python.
translations.work.stack86.architecture.item.2: Execution stays in the browser, because a held-down Step button cannot wait for the network.
translations.work.stack86.architecture.item.3: Every stage is a filter, and each language takes its chain from one registry, so the whole back half is shared.
translations.work.stack86.architecture.item.4: I wrote the CQRS layer instead of taking MediatR: two interfaces and a dispatcher were all it needed.
translations.work.stack86.domain.title: Domain design
translations.work.stack86.domain.text.1: One small intermediate representation that every language has to fit into.
translations.work.stack86.domain.ddd.label: Not a DDD domain, on purpose
translations.work.stack86.domain.ddd.text: A compiler is a pure function from source to assembly, with no state that outlives a request. The shared vocabulary here is the IR, not an aggregate.
translations.work.stack86.figure.pipeline.alt: Pipeline diagram: nine languages pass their own checks; C++ is transpiled to C and TypeScript to JavaScript; seven front ends lower everything to one intermediate representation, which is optimised, validated against the 8086 limits and emitted as 8086 assembly.
translations.work.stack86.figure.pipeline.caption: Nine languages in, one IR in the middle, one 8086 back end out.
translations.work.stack86.domain.item.1: Front ends know nothing about the 8086. They produce IR and diagnostics, nothing else.
translations.work.stack86.domain.item.2: Registers, segments and INT 21h live only behind the code generator.
translations.work.stack86.domain.item.3: Wiring a language in is one registry entry, not a special case.
translations.work.stack86.flow.title: Data and control flow
translations.work.stack86.flow.text.1: One build, from the keystroke to the stepping emulator.
translations.work.stack86.figure.build.alt: Sequence diagram: the workbench posts the files; licence, scope, rate limit and the trial rule are checked; the pipeline streams build log lines as NDJSON while each toolchain check runs behind a circuit breaker, a retry and a timeout; the assembly arrives last and the emulator steps it locally; if a toolchain keeps failing, the circuit opens and the build fails fast.
translations.work.stack86.figure.build.caption: The log moves while the stages run; after that, every step is a local function call.
translations.work.stack86.testing.title: Testing strategy
translations.work.stack86.testing.text.1: 956 backend tests, 864 frontend specs, 100 end to end, and a build that fails on any warning.
translations.work.stack86.testing.item.1: A pipeline stage or a front end is a unit test. Routing, auth or the database make it an integration test.
translations.work.stack86.testing.item.2: Green tests did not catch the editor collapsing to five pixels, so I keep Playwright screenshots next to them.
translations.work.stack86.testing.item.3: StyleCop and ESLint with warnings as errors, and no escape hatch to any in either language.
translations.work.stack86.changes.title: What I would change
translations.work.stack86.changes.item.1: No register allocator yet: every value gets a stack slot, so the assembly is two to three times longer than it needs to be.
translations.work.stack86.changes.item.2: The optimiser is a single copy-propagation pass. Constant folding and dead-store elimination are still missing.
translations.work.stack86.changes.item.4: A toolchain missing on the server looks like a compiler bug, not a missing dependency.
translations.work.stack86.changes.item.5: The languages are not equally deep, and the language picker should say so.
translations.work.taskly.tagline.text: Project and issue tracking with a Kanban board, epics, time tracking, reporting and real-time notifications, on .NET 10 and Angular 22.
translations.work.taskly.summary.text: A CQRS backend where controllers only dispatch, a domain that refuses silent overwrites, and a board that updates live over SignalR.
translations.work.taskly.note.text: Deletion is a state, not an event. Every entity is soft-deleted, so "who removed this and when" is a query, not a restore from backup.

translations.work.taskly.fact.4.label: Real time
translations.work.taskly.fact.4.value: SignalR, with per-user groups and eight background workers
translations.work.taskly.fact.5.label: Tests

translations.work.taskly.page.text: Taskly in detail: a CQRS backend over EF Core with soft delete and optimistic concurrency, OpenIddict authentication, SignalR notifications, and an Angular 22 client on signal stores.

translations.work.taskly.overview.usecase.text: Someone triages the overnight cards, moves three onto the board and starts a timer. Everything underneath exists so two people editing the same task never silently lose an edit.
translations.work.taskly.overview.item.2: Issues with priority, status, labels, epics and a position on the board
translations.work.taskly.overview.item.3: Board, backlog, epic and resolved views for every project
translations.work.taskly.overview.item.6: Time tracking, a calendar and reporting charts
translations.work.taskly.overview.item.7: Live notifications, deadline reminders and a weekly digest

translations.work.taskly.architecture.title: Architecture
translations.work.taskly.architecture.text.1: Six layers, one direction, and controllers that only dispatch.
translations.work.taskly.figure.architecture.alt: Architecture diagram: the browser calls Taskly.Web over HTTPS and gets notifications over SignalR; Web, Api, Logic and Data depend strictly downward onto SQL Server; Common and Contracts are shared; a separate admin app calls the API over HTTP.
translations.work.taskly.figure.architecture.caption: Every arrow points down; the admin app is a client of the API, not a back door.
translations.work.taskly.architecture.item.1: A project may only reference the layer below it, so any handler can be tested against a fake.
translations.work.taskly.architecture.item.2: A controller builds a command or a query and dispatches it. Permissions come from attributes, not from checks inside handlers.
translations.work.taskly.architecture.item.3: The Angular client is standalone components on signal stores, one per domain slice, rendered on the server.
translations.work.taskly.architecture.item.4: I wrote the CQRS layer, the Result type and a small mapper myself: cheaper to own than to configure.
translations.work.taskly.domain.title: Domain design
translations.work.taskly.domain.text.1: Two aggregates, and two rules the database enforces instead of convention.
translations.work.taskly.figure.erd.alt: Entity relationship diagram: projects have contributors and task items, task items have subtasks, and comments, time entries and attachments belong to a task item or a subtask; notifications, system tasks and deletion logs reference rows by id only.
translations.work.taskly.figure.erd.caption: The tables behind the board. SD marks soft delete, RV a row version.
translations.work.taskly.domain.item.1: Project and TaskItem are the aggregate roots. Handlers load and save only those.
translations.work.taskly.domain.item.2: Each save carries the row version the client read, so an edit made against a stale copy is refused with a 409.
translations.work.taskly.domain.item.3: A global query filter makes delete a flag. Hard delete is for administrators only.
translations.work.taskly.domain.item.4: One specification per entity keeps queries out of the handlers.
translations.work.taskly.flow.title: Data and control flow
translations.work.taskly.flow.text.1: One card moved on the board, followed to the other browser that sees it.
translations.work.taskly.figure.cardmove.alt: Sequence diagram: the board moves the card at once and sends a transition with the row version it read; the handler loads the card, applies the rules and saves only if that version still matches, then tells every contributor’s board over SignalR, and the other board reloads; if someone saved first, the API answers 409 and the board reloads to show their version.
translations.work.taskly.figure.cardmove.caption: Checked against what the mover saw, then shown to everyone with the board open.
translations.work.taskly.flow.text.2: A board column loads every card and subtask in one batch request, not one per card. Eight background services dispatch the same commands controllers do, so a trial ends without anyone clicking anything.
translations.work.taskly.testing.title: Testing strategy
translations.work.taskly.testing.text.1: 3,666 backend test methods and 2,241 frontend specs, with the handler as the unit.
translations.work.taskly.testing.item.1: A handler is tested with a fake repository and a principal, and asserted through its Result.
translations.work.taskly.testing.item.2: Routing, auth or the database make it an integration test by definition.
translations.work.taskly.testing.callout.label: What this got wrong
translations.work.taskly.testing.callout.text: CI ran lint, build and unit tests, but no end-to-end stage. Twenty-nine Playwright tests sat red for weeks. A gate that does not run is not a gate.
translations.work.taskly.changes.title: What I would change
translations.work.taskly.changes.item.1: Tasks and workflows share their shapes but diverged in code. One generic feature would remove about a thousand lines.
translations.work.taskly.changes.item.2: The reflective mapper was right at ten DTOs and is wrong at fifty: slower, and a rename only fails at runtime.
translations.work.taskly.changes.item.6: Subtasks do not send their row version or broadcast their moves yet. The task path is the template to copy.
translations.work.taskly.changes.item.7: A reorder writes one UPDATE per card inside a transaction. A single CASE statement would make it one round trip.
translations.work.taskly.changes.item.4: Permissions live in the API and are mirrored in the client. Sending them with the session would remove the drift.

translations.pillar.1.title: Keep the core independent
translations.pillar.1.text: The part of a system that holds the rules should not depend on what surrounds it. Then changing the screen or the storage never puts the rules at risk.
translations.pillar.2.title: Tests do not tell you it looks right
translations.pillar.2.text: A passing suite tells me the logic works, not that the screen is usable. I answer the second question by looking.
translations.pillar.3.title: Faster drafts, same bar
translations.pillar.3.text: I use AI tooling every day and it makes me faster. It has not lowered the bar a change has to clear before it ships.
translations.about.eyebrow.label: About
translations.about.text.1: For 4+ years I have built cloud accounting SaaS for the Nordic market: four .NET and Angular microservices talking over Azure Service Bus with Rebus sagas and CQRS, each with its own multi-tenant SQL Server.
translations.about.text.2: Lately: moving a .NET Framework 4.8 monolith to .NET 8 piece by piece and its Knockout.js frontend to React 19, every step behind a feature flag.
translations.about.text.3: I grew up between two languages and now work in three. I like real constraints, code someone can still read in a year, and finding out early when I am wrong.
translations.hero.title: I build web applications end to end, from the database to the browser.
translations.hero.text: By day: 4+ years of .NET, Angular, React and Azure on cloud accounting products for the Nordic market. The four projects below nobody ordered. I built them to find out how a compiler reads code, and what a processor does between two instructions.
translations.home.page.title: Christian-Ioan Szasz - Full-Stack Engineer Portfolio
translations.home.page.description: Software engineer in Sibiu, Romania. 4+ years of .NET, Angular, React and Azure on cloud accounting products for the Nordic market, and four side projects of my own: a compiler, a CPU simulator, a task tracker and this site.
translations.profile.eyebrow.label: About me
translations.profile.title: Engineer by trade, curious by default.
translations.profile.text.1: Software engineer in Sibiu, Romania. 4+ years building cloud accounting products for the Nordic market, and a standing habit of rebuilding things myself to find out how they actually work.
translations.profile.text.2: My degrees are in computer science and electrical engineering, and the work I do for myself sits where they meet: compilers, an 8086 emulator, the gap between a line of source and a register changing value.

translations.cookies.text: This website uses no cookies and employs no third-party analytics or advertising services. No third-party scripts, fonts or tracking technologies are loaded. A small amount of information is stored locally on your device to remember your preferences, and, only with your consent, an anonymous record of visits and of how the website is used is maintained. This notice explains both.
translations.cookies.stored.title: Information stored on your device
translations.cookies.stored.text: To remember your preferences, the website stores a small amount of information locally within your browser. This is limited to your selected display theme, your response to the consent request, and the date of your most recent recorded visit. This information remains on your device until you clear this website's site data, is not transmitted with any request, and cannot be used to identify or track you.
translations.cookies.counter.title: Visit statistics
translations.cookies.counter.text.short: With your consent, the website keeps an anonymous visit count, a country breakdown and a record of how it is used, none of it identifying. No advertising identifiers or visitor profiles are created. Retention periods and the legal basis are set out in the {$START_LINK}privacy policy{$CLOSE_LINK}. If you decline, nothing is recorded.
translations.cookies.breakdown.title: Visits by country
translations.cookies.attribution.text: Country information is derived from the IP-to-country database provided by {$START_LINK}DB-IP{$CLOSE_LINK}, used under the Creative Commons Attribution licence.
translations.cookies.consent.title: Consent
translations.cookies.consent.text: On your first visit, a notice requests your consent to the visit statistics described above. If you accept, they operate as set out here; if you decline, nothing is recorded and your network address is not processed. Your choice is retained so that the request is not repeated.
translations.cookies.remove.title: Withdrawing consent and removing information
translations.cookies.remove.text: You may withdraw your consent and remove all information held on your device at any time by clearing this website's site data through your browser settings. Browsing in a private window will similarly discard it once the window is closed.
translations.cookies.links.title: External links
translations.cookies.links.text: This website contains links to external services, including GitHub and LinkedIn. These are operated by third parties under their own terms and privacy practices, for which no responsibility is accepted. No content is loaded from them unless you choose to follow a link.
translations.cookies.contact.title: Contact
translations.cookies.contact.text: For any question regarding this notice, please contact {$START_LINK} christian.ioan.szasz@gmail.com{$CLOSE_LINK}.
translations.privacy.text: This is the personal portfolio of Christian-Ioan Szasz. It is designed to respect the privacy of its visitors: it requires no account, serves no advertising, uses no third-party analytics service, and loads no third-party trackers. This policy sets out the limited processing that takes place and the rights available to you.
translations.privacy.collect.title: Information collected
translations.privacy.collect.text: No information that identifies you is collected. The website requests no name, email address or account, and loads no third-party analytics, advertising or social-media trackers. Its pages are static and served directly to your browser.
translations.privacy.counter.title: Visit statistics
translations.privacy.counter.text: Only with your consent does the website maintain an anonymous count of visits and a breakdown of visitors' countries, together with an anonymous record of how the website is used: which pages and sections are reached, and whether the curriculum vitae is opened or downloaded. These records carry no identifier, are counted only as totals, and cannot be linked to you or to one another. The usage record is kept for 30 days and then deleted. The visit count and the country breakdown are running totals and are not deleted, because a total is a number that refers to no one. The approximate country is determined on the server from your network address, which is used solely for that purpose and discarded immediately; the website never stores, records or shares it. If you do not consent, nothing is recorded and your network address is not processed.
translations.privacy.storage.title: Information stored on your device
translations.privacy.storage.text: A small amount of information is stored on your device to remember your preferences, namely your display theme, your response to the consent request, and the date of your most recent recorded visit. It remains on your device and is not transmitted with any request. Further detail is provided in the {$START_TAG_BUTTON}cookies and storage notice{$CLOSE_TAG_BUTTON}.
translations.privacy.hosting.title: Hosting
translations.privacy.hosting.text: The website and the service that maintains the visit statistics are hosted on Microsoft Azure. The statistics service and its records remain within the European Union; the pages themselves are delivered from locations near each visitor, which may lie outside it. Microsoft processes requests on the author's behalf solely in order to provide the website, under data protection terms that include the safeguards the General Data Protection Regulation requires for such transfers. Technical error reports produced by the statistics service contain no information that identifies any visitor; they are retained for no longer than 30 days and are summarised for the author by email.
translations.privacy.hosting.demos: When you open the website, your browser also asks the statistics service and the live demonstrations, which are hosted in the same way, to start, so that they are ready should you use them. These requests carry no identifier, are made whether or not you consent to the visit statistics, and are not recorded.
translations.privacy.basis.title: Lawful basis
translations.privacy.basis.text: The only optional processing, the visit and usage statistics and the associated country lookup, is carried out on the basis of your consent under Article 6(1)(a) of the General Data Protection Regulation. You may withdraw that consent at any time by clearing the site data, after which consent will be requested again.
translations.privacy.rights.title: Your rights
translations.privacy.rights.text: As no information identifying you is held, there is no personal record to access, rectify or export. You may nonetheless:
translations.privacy.rights.item.1: Withdraw your consent at any time by clearing this website's site data.
translations.privacy.rights.item.2: Remove all information stored on your device through your browser settings.
translations.privacy.rights.item.3: Contact the address below with any question regarding this policy.
translations.privacy.rights.item.4: Lodge a complaint with a data protection supervisory authority, in particular the National Supervisory Authority for Personal Data Processing (ANSPDCP) in Romania or the authority of your place of residence.
translations.privacy.security.title: Security
translations.privacy.security.text: The website is served exclusively over an encrypted connection. As it offers no accounts, it holds no passwords or other credentials that could be exposed.
translations.privacy.children.title: Children
translations.privacy.children.text: The website is not directed at children. As it collects no information that identifies any visitor, it holds none concerning children.
translations.privacy.controller.title: Data controller
translations.privacy.controller.text: The data controller is Christian-Ioan Szasz. Any privacy enquiry may be addressed to {$START_LINK} christian.ioan.szasz@gmail.com{$CLOSE_LINK}.
translations.privacy.changes.title: Changes to this policy
translations.privacy.changes.text: Should the website's processing of data change, this policy will be updated and the date shown above amended accordingly.
